chapter: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
title: Lester Young as a loner who is warm to those he likes
summary: Thompson explains that Lester was reserved with people who did not understand the music but warm to musicians he liked.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: But Lester in those days -- Lester wasn't exactly as approachable musician as some other musicians, was he? I mean, wasn't -- Lester was a loner in a way, was he not?
Yes, but you see, that's the strange

part about it. Lester was a loner to people who didn't know him, and he only -- he kept himself restricted to only the people he wanted to know. He only got warm with people he wanted to know, because most of the people didn't understand the music, and didn't appreciate him and showed signs of it, so he rebelled against it.

But a musician who could play fairly well, or was good enough to make an impression on him, or that he liked to play with, and that he heard something he liked, he was very warm. He was not the same cold person that he seemed to be to other people.

And that's the way -- it's like a clique, click if you want to call it, whatever. But it's like sports or anything else, if you can do something well, you know, or if you can do something that someone else appreciates, and they do the same thing, you have a natural tendency.

It's just like you and I talking here. You have an appreciation as an interviewer of what I'm doing and what others are doing that makes you interested. Whereas someone else who didn't have an appreciation for it wouldn't care if they talked to me ever about it.
Or wouldn't care if I existed.
